title: The citadel
hookLine: a mind free from passions is a citadel, Marcus writes (Meditations 8.48)

lines: A FORTRESS ON THE HIGH GROUND.
cards: Many old Greek cities had one: a fortress on the highest ground. When raiders came up the valley, the farmers and families ran uphill, through the gates, and the walls held.
In Athens it's the Acropolis, where the Parthenon still stands. Now picture an emperor in an army camp on the northern frontier, with a long war on his hands. He has no hill to run to.
So he writes himself a note about the one fortress nobody can take. Today: the citadel.

teach.b: Marcus Aurelius wrote his notebook in Greek, and in book eight he uses the word for a city's fortress, akropolis.
In George Long's translation, he writes that "the mind which is free from passions is a citadel". Nothing, he goes on, is more secure for a person to flee to.
Remember passions from last week: not all feeling, but the runaway kind, built on a mistaken judgment. So the citadel isn't a numb mind. It's a mind that hasn't said yes to the panic.
Earlier in the Meditations he makes the point another way. People look for retreats, houses in the country, the seashore, the mountains.
But you can retreat into yourself any time you like, and there's no quieter place. It doesn't take a vacation. It takes a minute.
The historian Pierre Hadot named a whole book about Marcus after this image, The Inner Citadel. And it gathers up this week. Zeno, in agreement.
The logos, the pattern. Sympatheia, all woven. Hierocles' circles, drawn in.
A bigger home around the smaller one. Amor fati, love what happens. Each one widened the view to the whole cosmos; the citadel brings it back to one quiet room inside you.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD, A STEADY CENTER.
teach.b: That's the Stoic shape: the biggest possible world, and a small, steady center from which to meet it. One honest note.
Marcus wrote this for himself, not for us, and some readers hear a man reminding himself because he kept forgetting.
If so, the citadel wasn't a place he lived. It was a place he kept walking back to.

how: Stoic practitioners take short pauses during the day to retreat inward, as Marcus Aurelius describes, instead of waiting for a vacation to find calm.

o: a strong will that pushes every feeling away
a sacred temple on the hill above a Greek city
a mind free of runaway passions, a refuge inside you

games.q: the Stoic world — tap the pairs.
p: the high fortress of a city

s: Marcus's citadel is a mind that feels nothing
it's a mind free of runaway passions, not of all feeling.
Marcus wrote his notebook in Greek
the word he uses for citadel is akropolis.
Marcus says the best retreat is a house in the country
he says you can retreat into yourself any time, and it's the quietest place.

games.q: you're an emperor at war, with no time off. where does Marcus say to retreat?
games.why: people seek country houses and seashores, he writes, but you can retreat into yourself whenever you like.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and picture a path going uphill; walk it to a gate at the top, step through, and let it close behind you.
The noise of the day is outside the walls now: you can still hear it, it just can't come in. Rest inside, breathing.

wordCard.voice: The citadel. Marcus Aurelius's image for a mind free from runaway passions: a fortress you can retreat into anytime.

orig.note: Greek: the high city, a fortress; Marcus's word for the free mind in Meditations 8.48.

carryVoice: Your line: one quiet room inside you. That's the week in the Stoic world; next week, the Stoics honestly. Rest well.
